South Carolina property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • Taxpayer must give the assessor written notice of objection within 90 days after the assessor mails the property tax assessment notice. (SC Code 12-60-2510(A)(3); source)
  • In years with no assessment notice, a taxpayer may appeal the fair market value, assessment ratio and assessment at any time, in writing to the assessor. (SC Code 12-60-2510(A)(4); source)
  • A written request to meet with the assessor within the 12-60-2510 time limits is a notice of objection; the taxpayer has 30 days after the conference to file a written protest with the assessor. (SC Code 12-60-2520; source)
  • Within 30 days after the county board's written decision, the taxpayer or assessor may request a contested case hearing before the Administrative Law Court. (SC Code 12-60-2540(A); source)
  • Legal residence (owner-occupied, up to 5 contiguous acres) is assessed at 4% of fair market value. (SC Code 12-43-220(c)(1); source)
  • Each county must appraise and equalize property once every fifth year. (SC Code 12-43-217(A); source)
  • Real property sold at a delinquent tax sale may be redeemed within 12 months by the defaulting taxpayer, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor. (SC Code 12-51-90(A); source)
  • Redemption interest on the bid: 3% in months 1-3, 6% in months 4-6, 9% in months 7-9, 12% in months 10-12, not exceeding the bid submitted for the forfeited land commission. (SC Code 12-51-90(B); source)

What the official sources say

  • First $50,000 of fair market value of the dwelling place is exempt from county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate taxes for owners who are 65+ (SC resident 1+ year), totally and permanently disabled, or legally blind. (SC Code 12-37-250(A)(1); source)
  • Failure to apply constitutes a waiver of the exemption for that year; application may be made in person, by mail with documentation, or online where the auditor has records. (SC Code 12-37-250; source)
  • 'Dwelling place' means the permanent home and legal residence of the applicant. (SC Code 12-37-250(A)(5); source)
  • Owner must hold fee simple title or a life estate; jointly owned by spouses qualifies if either meets the age/disability/blindness test. (SC Code 12-37-250(A)(1)-(2); source)

What is the South Carolina homestead exemption?

It exempts the first $50,000 of the fair market value of a dwelling place from county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate taxes for owners who are 65 or older, totally and permanently disabled, or legally blind. The rule is in S.C. Code 12-37-250.

It is a tax exemption on the home, not a creditor protection and not a freeze on the value. The South Carolina Department of Revenue describes it as a complete exemption from taxes on the first $50,000 of fair market value of your legal residence, and it is handled through the county auditor. You can read the statute on the Legislature's Chapter 37 page and the agency summary on the SCDOR exemptions page.

Who qualifies for the exemption?

An owner qualifies by age, disability or blindness, and by holding the right kind of title to the dwelling.

  • Age: a South Carolina resident for at least one year who turned 65 on or before December 31.
  • Disability: someone classified as totally and permanently disabled by a state or federal agency. A person who is not classified can ask the state Vocational Rehabilitation agency to evaluate the claim.
  • Blindness: a person who is legally blind as defined in Section 43-25-20.
  • Title: the owner needs complete fee simple title or a life estate. Life estates created by will count.

A home owned jointly by spouses qualifies when either spouse meets the test before January 1 of the tax year and the one-year residency requirement is met. The statute defines permanent and total disability as the inability to do substantial gainful work because of a medically determinable impairment lasting, or expected to last, at least 12 continuous months or ending in death.

How do you apply, and by when?

Apply in writing to the county auditor before July 16 of the tax year. An application filed after July 15 normally applies to the next year, with one exception for filings made before the first penalty date.

The statute allows three routes: in person at the auditor's office, by mail with proof of age, disability or blindness, or online where the auditor can check official records. Failing to apply waives the exemption for that year. The SCDOR says the individual form is PT-401I and that processing is currently 10 to 12 weeks, with MyDORWAY as the fastest filing method.

ItemWhat the sources say
Exempt amountFirst $50,000 of fair market value (12-37-250(A)(1))
Filing officeCounty auditor, with notice to the municipality
Written application cutoffBefore July 16 of the tax year
Individual formPT-401I (SCDOR)
Refund claimsWithin two years of the date taxes were paid (SCDOR)
Rollback periodCurrent year plus five preceding years (SCDOR)

The SCDOR page also notes that for tax year 2026 the state temporarily authorized an additional amount for certain recipients, and the county auditor decides whether it applies to you.

How is the homestead exemption different from the 4 percent legal residence rate?

They are two separate breaks. The 4 percent legal residence assessment lowers the taxable share of value for an owner-occupied home, while the homestead exemption removes the first $50,000 of value for qualifying seniors, disabled owners and blind owners.

The SCDOR states that the legal residence must be approved before a real estate exemption is granted, and the legal residence application goes through the county assessor. Under 12-43-220(c), the 4 percent ratio covers the home and up to five contiguous acres that the owner occupies as a legal residence. Other real property is assessed at 6 percent.

  • The legal residence application must be made before the first penalty date for the first tax year the owner claims it.
  • A residence rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year loses the 4 percent rate.
  • An owner who is found ineligible, or who fails to tell the assessor within six months of losing eligibility, can owe a penalty of 100 percent of the tax plus interest at one-half of one percent per month.

What happens to the exemption when you sell the house?

The exemption belongs to the owner's permanent home, so it stops with the sale and a buyer does not inherit it. The statute defines the dwelling place as the applicant's permanent home and legal residence.

A seller who moves in South Carolina can claim the exemption on the new residence, and a surviving spouse who moves must tell the auditor of the new address. A surviving spouse can also keep the exemption on the current home if they take complete fee simple title or a life estate within nine months of the death, and it continues while the spouse stays unmarried and uses it as a permanent home (12-37-250(D)).

The statute also says the exemption does not trigger a reassessment of the property. The five-year reappraisal cycle in 12-43-217 still runs on its own schedule, and a county may postpone implementing new values by one tax year.

How do taxes get handled at closing in South Carolina?

Real estate taxes are billed a year behind and are due between September 30 and January 15, so the closing statement usually splits the year between buyer and seller. The statute puts the penalty at 3 percent after January 15, with 7 percent more after February 2 and another 5 percent after March 17 (12-45-70 and 12-45-180).

If title changes after assessment, a new owner can ask the auditor to apportion the taxes and costs owed by the original owner before any tax-execution sale (12-45-140). When title transfers during the year and the notice went to the prior owner, the treasurer must waive penalties if the current owner never got a timely notice (12-45-180(B)).

The deed also carries a recording fee of $1.85 per $500 of value, made up of $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county (12-24-10). The grantor generally owes it (12-24-20). Confirm the numbers with your closing attorney and county office.

Can owners with other situations get relief?

Yes, several other exemptions exist, each with its own rules and form.

  • Disabled veterans: a dwelling with a lot not exceeding five acres.
  • Paraplegic or hemiplegic persons: a dwelling and lot up to one acre.
  • Medal of Honor or former prisoner of war recipients: a dwelling and lot up to one acre.
  • Disabled law enforcement officers and firefighters with service-connected disability: a dwelling with a lot not exceeding five acres.

These come from 12-37-220(B) and the SCDOR page. Ask your county auditor which fits before you list a home, since the right exemption can lower the carrying cost while you are waiting to sell.

Does the exemption cover mobile homes or shared ownership?

Yes in some cases. An owner of a mobile home on leased land may receive the exemption against personal property taxes under the same procedures, but cannot receive both the real and the personal property exemption in the same year (12-37-250(B)).

An owner-lessee who will own the home when the lease ends qualifies as though holding fee simple or a life estate. A part owner gets the owned percentage of the full exemption, with ownership under 5 percent treated as 5 percent, and the exemption cannot exceed the value of that interest (12-37-250(J)). Heirs who inherit a share of a parent's home should keep this in mind before a sale.

More questions about South Carolina Homestead Exemption

How much is the South Carolina homestead exemption?

The first $50,000 of the fair market value of your dwelling place is exempt from county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate taxes, under S.C. Code 12-37-250(A)(1).

What age do you have to be?

You must be 65 by December 31 and have lived in South Carolina for at least one year. Totally and permanently disabled and legally blind owners qualify without the age test.

When is the application deadline?

Written applications must be made before July 16 of the tax year. A later application generally takes effect the following year.

Does a buyer keep my homestead exemption?

No. The exemption applies to the applicant's permanent home and legal residence, so a buyer must qualify on their own and apply to the county auditor.

Does the exemption apply to a rental?

The 4 percent legal residence rate is lost if the home is rented more than 72 days in a calendar year, and the homestead exemption requires the home to be the owner's permanent residence.

content:
South Carolina Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Cash Home Buyers in South Carolina
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a South Carolina Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House sale
  • Turn the South Carolina Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a South Carolina House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Landlord may obtain evictions in magistrate's or circuit court without posting bond. (SC Code 27-40-710(C); source)
  • Evicted tenant's property placed on a public street is removed after 48 hours (excluding weekends/holidays); eviction notice must inform the tenant. (SC Code 27-40-710(D); source)
  • Week-to-week tenancy terminable on 7 days written notice; month-to-month on 30 days. (SC Code 27-40-770(a)-(b); source)
Selling in South Carolina?
We buy South Carolina houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How does an eviction work in South Carolina?

A South Carolina landlord ends a tenancy with written notice, then asks a magistrate for a rule to show cause, and only a court-issued writ lets the tenant be removed. The landlord cannot change locks or shut off water to force the issue.

The two statutes that matter are Chapter 40 of Title 27 (the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act) and Chapter 37 of Title 27 (ejectment of tenants). The first says when a lease can be ended. The second sets the court steps. If you own a rented house and are thinking of selling it, you need to know where a tenant sits on that path, because it shapes what a buyer will pay for and when the keys can change hands.

Read the primary text at the South Carolina Legislature's Chapter 40 page and the Chapter 37 page.

What notice comes before a South Carolina eviction case?

The notice depends on the reason: five days for unpaid rent, fourteen days for most other lease breaches, and thirty or seven days to end a periodic tenancy. Each must be written.

SituationNotice or periodStatute
Rent unpaidFive days from the due date, with written notice of nonpayment and intent to end27-40-710(B)
Other lease breach not fixedTermination no sooner than 14 days after the tenant receives the notice27-40-710(A)
Week-to-week tenancyAt least 7 days written notice27-40-770(a)
Month-to-month tenancyAt least 30 days written notice27-40-770(b)
Tenant response to rule to show cause10 days after service27-37-20

The lease can carry the nonpayment warning itself. The statute even supplies the sentence a lease must contain about the five-day window, so a landlord should check that wording before relying on it.

What happens in magistrate court?

The landlord applies to the magistrate, who issues a rule telling the tenant to leave or appear and explain why not within ten days of service. If the tenant does nothing, a warrant of ejectment follows.

Service is where many South Carolina cases slow down. The statute lets the rule be served like a summons. If the home looks abandoned for 15 days or more, the rule may be fixed to the most visible part of the premises. After two failed attempts at least 48 hours apart, and at times at least eight hours apart, it may be posted and mailed through the clerk, and mailed service counts as complete ten days after mailing (27-37-30).

If the tenant appears and contests, the magistrate hears the matter like other civil cases, and either side may ask for a jury. Many landlords build a few weeks of slack into any closing date for this reason.

  • Rent keeps accruing at the old rate while the tenant stays, and taking rent does not give up the right to eject (27-37-150).
  • A judgment for the landlord leads to a writ of ejectment within five days (27-37-100).
  • A judgment for the tenant lets the tenant stay until the tenancy ends by agreement or law, or rent goes unpaid (27-37-110).

Who physically removes a tenant, and how fast?

A constable or deputy sheriff carries out the writ, and the occupants get 24 hours to leave voluntarily after it is presented. Only a deputy sheriff, not a constable, may force entry, and then only by the least destructive means (27-37-160).

The officer may delay removal for an ill or elderly tenant. When a tenant's belongings are set out on a public street, they are removed after 48 hours, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and holidays, and the eviction notice must tell the tenant so (27-40-710(D)).

An appeal is possible, but it does not stop the ejectment unless the tenant posts an appeal bond, and the appeal is dismissed if that bond is not filed within five days after service of the notice of appeal (27-37-120 and 27-37-130). A landlord can bring the action in magistrate's or circuit court without posting a bond (27-40-710(C)).

What can a landlord not do in South Carolina?

A landlord may not recover possession by cutting off essential services or any other self-help, except where the tenant has abandoned, surrendered or the tenancy has properly ended (27-40-760).

Several other rules protect tenants during a sale or an eviction:

  • Entry needs 24 hours notice at reasonable times, with emergencies excepted (27-40-530). That matters for showings and inspections.
  • Retaliation is barred. A tenant who wants to raise it as a defense to a rule to vacate must notify the landlord in writing within ten days of service, and a retaliating landlord can owe up to three months rent or treble damages (27-40-910).
  • Unexplained absence for 15 days after a rent default can be treated as abandonment, and left property valued at $500 or less may be disposed of under the conditions in 27-40-730.

A willful holdover after a lease ends can cost the tenant up to three months periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees (27-40-770(c)).

How does an eviction affect selling a rented house in South Carolina?

A pending case does not stop you from selling, but it changes the timeline and the type of buyer. Most financed buyers want a vacant house or a clean lease, which is why many owners with a tenant in default look at an as-is cash sale.

Think through these points before you list or sign a contract:

  • If a tenant has a valid lease, the deposit duties travel with the sale. A seller who conveys in good faith is relieved of later liability after written notice to the tenant, but stays responsible for the deposit unless it is transferred and the tenant is told (27-40-410 and 27-40-450).
  • Owner or agent contact details must be kept current and bind a successor owner (27-40-420(b)). Give the buyer that information in writing.
  • A buyer who does not want the tenant can only take the house vacant if the tenancy has ended lawfully. Do not promise a delivery date that depends on a court calendar you do not control.

When a tenant is current and the lease runs for months, selling subject to the lease may be the simpler route. When the tenant is in default or holding over, owners often prefer to sell the house with the tenant issue priced in.

What should a landlord check on a South Carolina property before selling?

Start with the lease, the rent ledger and the deposit record, then confirm your property tax status with the county.

Rented houses are not treated like owner homes for tax purposes. The 4 percent legal residence ratio does not apply to a residence rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year, and a property found ineligible can face a 100 percent penalty on the tax plus interest of one-half of one percent per month (12-43-220(c)). Other real property is assessed at 6 percent, so a rental can carry a heavier bill than the owner's own home would.

Property taxes are payable between September 30 and January 15. Penalties of 3 percent, then 7 percent more after February 2 and 5 percent more after March 17 follow (12-45-70 and 12-45-180). Ask the county auditor and treasurer for the current year's figures before a closing.

Where can a landlord or tenant get official help?

The best starting points are the county magistrate's office, which accepts the filings, and the primary statutes themselves.

Court clerks cannot give legal advice, so a landlord with a complicated case, a tenant claiming retaliation or a holdover dispute should speak with a South Carolina attorney. If you want to compare notes on how a sale could work around a tenant situation, our team can walk through it with you at no obligation, and you can read the statute text in full first.

More questions about South Carolina Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a South Carolina eviction take?

There is no fixed total, because it depends on service and whether the tenant contests. The statutory pieces are a five-day or fourteen-day notice, a ten-day window after the rule is served, a writ within five days of a landlord win, and 24 hours to leave once the officer presents the writ.

Can a landlord lock a tenant out in South Carolina?

No. Section 27-40-760 bars recovering possession by self-help or by willfully cutting essential services, except for abandonment, surrender or proper termination.

How much notice ends a month-to-month lease?

Either side must give at least thirty days of written notice before the termination date under 27-40-770(b). A week-to-week tenancy needs at least seven days.

Can I sell a house while a tenant is being evicted?

Yes, nothing in the statutes bars a sale during a case. The buyer takes the property subject to the court process, and the deposit rules in 27-40-410 and 27-40-450 still apply to what is owed the tenant.

What happens to a tenant's belongings after an eviction?

Property placed on a public street is removed after 48 hours, not counting weekends and holidays. Abandoned property valued at $500 or less may be disposed of under 27-40-730 once its conditions are met.

What the official sources say

  • In counties other than the 25 listed counties (including Charleston, Greenville, Richland, Horry), the clerk of court performs the register of deeds duties; the listed counties have a register of deeds. (SC Code 30-5-10(A); source)
  • Before recording, a deed must be proved by a subscribing witness affidavit or acknowledged by the grantor in the presence of two witnesses before an officer competent to administer oaths. (SC Code 30-5-30; source)
  • The register of deeds records instruments in the order presented, once execution is proved. (SC Code Title 30, Ch. 5; source)
  • The deed recording fee ($1.85 per $500) is collected before recording, with an affidavit of value. (SC Code 12-24-10, 12-24-70; source)
